canon.title: Athens, 470–322 BC
canon.about: Classical facts of Athens from the boyhood of Socrates to the deaths of Aristotle and Demosthenes: philosophy foremost (Socrates and his pupils, the sophists, the Academy and the Lyceum), with the politics and wars that framed it, the theatre that mocked it, and the art of Pericles' Athens. Dates are years BC written as astronomical years in the proleptic Julian calendar (399 BC is -0398); an Athenian year ran from midsummer to midsummer, so most dates are years, intervals of two years, or approximate. Its selection is that of the surviving literature: what Plato, Xenophon, Thucydides, Aristotle's biographers, Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius chose to tell, centred on a few famous men of one city; women, slaves, metics other than the famous, and the rest of Greece appear only where these authors bring them in, and some occasions rest on late anecdote, which the confidences say. A seed canon, drafted from general knowledge by a language model, each assertion naming the ancient or modern source it is to be checked against; none is checked yet.

beings.name: Speusippus
beings.note: Plato's nephew; scholarch of the Academy 347-339.

beings.name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
beings.note: Dated c. 390-337 BC by Apollodorus' reckoning as usually corrected; older handbooks give c. 408-355.

beings.name: Critias
beings.note: Leader of the Thirty; a cousin of Plato's mother.

beings.name: Hermias of Atarneus
beings.note: Tyrant of Atarneus and Assos; executed by the Persians c. 341 BC.

beings.name: Athens (the Athenian state: its assembly, courts and army)

occasions.label: The Parthenon begun, in Pericles' programme of building, with Phidias overseeing the works
The panhellenic colony of Thurii founded under Pericles; Protagoras writes its laws
occasions.note: Protagoras's laws for Thurii rest on Heraclides Ponticus, cited by Diogenes Laertius (IX.50).

occasions.label: The Samian War: Sophocles among the generals with Pericles
Phidias's gold and ivory Athena Parthenos dedicated, at the Great Panathenaia
occasions.note: In the archonship of Theodorus, 438/437 (Philochorus); the Great Panathenaia fell in Hekatombaion, July-August.

occasions.label: Phidias prosecuted over the gold and ivory of the Athena, in an attack aimed at Pericles
occasions.note: Dated here by Philochorus, in the year of the dedication, 438/437, after which Phidias went to Elis; Plutarch puts it on the eve of the war, c. 432, and has him die in prison.

occasions.label: Anaxagoras prosecuted for impiety, defended by Pericles, leaves Athens for Lampsacus
occasions.note: Dated c. 433/432 by Plutarch's placing among the attacks on Pericles' friends, after the decree of Diopeithes; others put it in 437/436 or the 450s.

occasions.label: At the battle of Potidaea Socrates saves the wounded Alcibiades
At the City Dionysia Euripides' Medea is placed third, behind Euphorion and Sophocles
Pericles' funeral oration for the dead of the first year of the war
occasions.note: Winter 431/430; the words are Thucydides' (2.35-46).

occasions.label: In the plague and the invasion the Athenians depose and fine Pericles; they re-elect him soon after
occasions.note: In the second summer of the war, after the second invasion and the plague (Thucydides 2.59-65).

occasions.label: Protagoras praises the composure of Pericles at the deaths of his two sons
occasions.note: Protagoras fr. 9 DK, preserved in the Consolation to Apollonius ascribed to Plutarch.

occasions.label: Death of Pericles, of the plague
occasions.note: He outlived the outbreak of the war by two years and six months (Thucydides 2.65.6): autumn 429.

occasions.label: Death of Anaxagoras
Gorgias, on an embassy from Leontini, dazzles the Athenian assembly and wins an alliance
Aristophanes' Acharnians, with Euripides on stage lending rags, wins first prize
In the rout at Delium Socrates retreats steadily, Alcibiades on horseback beside him
Aristophanes' Clouds, with Socrates as a sophist in his thinkery, placed third
occasions.note: The text that survives is a partial revision of the play of 423.

occasions.label: Alcibiades elected general
Accused of profaning the Mysteries, Alcibiades is recalled from Sicily, flees to Sparta, and is condemned to death
Aristophanes' Thesmophoriazusae, a parody of Euripides and his plays
Plato, about twenty, becomes a follower of Socrates
occasions.note: Diogenes Laertius (III.5-6) has him burn his tragedies on hearing Socrates; the year is inferred from his age.

occasions.label: Alcibiades returns to Athens in triumph and is given command of all forces
occasions.note: On the day of the Plynteria, in Thargelion (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.4.12).

occasions.label: Death of Euripides at the court of Archelaus
occasions.note: In 407/406, before the Dionysia of 406. At the proagon of the next Dionysia Sophocles brought on his chorus in mourning (Life of Euripides).

occasions.label: After the defeat at Notium the Athenians remove Alcibiades from command; he withdraws to Thrace
occasions.note: Late 407 or early 406.

occasions.label: In the trial of the generals after Arginusae, Socrates, a prytanis, alone refuses to put the illegal motion
occasions.note: Autumn 406: the Apaturia, in Pyanepsion, fell during the proceedings (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.7.8).

occasions.label: Death of Sophocles
occasions.note: In 406/405, after the Dionysia of 406 and before the Frogs of 405 mourned him.

occasions.label: Aristophanes' Frogs wins first prize; its chorus mocks sitting idle by Socrates, chattering
Under the Thirty: Critias forbids Socrates to teach, Socrates refuses to arrest Leon of Salamis, and Plato, invited by his kinsmen to join them, is repelled
occasions.note: Plato's part rests on the Seventh Letter (324b-325a).

occasions.label: Alcibiades killed in Phrygia
Critias killed fighting the democrats at Munychia
Xenophon asks Socrates whether to join Cyrus; Socrates sends him to Delphi
occasions.note: Anabasis 3.1.5-7.

occasions.label: The trial of Socrates for impiety and corrupting the young; he names Aristophanes' comedy among the old slanders, and Plato offers surety for his fine
occasions.note: Apology 19c, 34a, 38b.

occasions.label: Death of Socrates by hemlock; Plato is absent, ill
occasions.note: Phaedo 59b.

occasions.label: Xenophon, an exile, fights with Agesilaus of Sparta against Athens and Thebes
occasions.note: Whether his exile was decreed in 399 or after Coronea is disputed.

occasions.label: Plato's first voyage to Sicily: he wins Dion and offends the elder Dionysius
occasions.note: The story that Dionysius had him sold as a slave (Diogenes Laertius III.18-20) is late and doubted.

occasions.label: Plato begins to teach in the grove of the Academy
occasions.note: The year, c. 387, is traditional.

occasions.label: Eudoxus comes to Athens with his pupils and joins the Academy's circle
occasions.note: Diogenes Laertius VIII.86-87; the date is inferred, and the later story that he led the Academy while Plato was in Sicily is contested.

occasions.label: Death of Dionysius I; his son Dionysius II succeeds
Aristotle, seventeen, joins the Academy, while Plato is away in Sicily
Plato's second voyage, at Dion's call, to make a philosopher of the young Dionysius II
Dionysius II banishes Dion and keeps Plato at court
Plato returns to the Academy, where Aristotle has been studying for two years
occasions.note: Aristotle's twenty years in the Academy (367-347) are well attested; his presence at this occasion is inferred from them.

occasions.label: Xenophon's son Gryllus falls at Mantinea fighting for Athens; Xenophon's exile is over
Plato's third voyage: he quarrels with Dionysius II over Dion and is held until Archytas obtains his release
occasions.note: Speusippus' presence rests on Plutarch (Dion 22).

occasions.label: Plato, back from Sicily, meets Dion at the Olympic games; Dion resolves on war
occasions.note: Seventh Letter 350b-c.

occasions.label: Aristotle's dialogue Gryllus, on rhetoric, against the school of Isocrates
occasions.note: Lost; known from Diogenes Laertius II.55 and Quintilian. Isocrates' pupil Cephisodorus answered Aristotle.

occasions.label: Dion sails from Zacynthus and takes Syracuse from Dionysius II
Dion murdered by Callippus, an Athenian of the Academy's circle
Demosthenes' First Philippic
occasions.note: The date, 351 or 349, is disputed.

occasions.label: Death of Plato; Speusippus succeeds him at the head of the Academy
occasions.note: In the archonship of Theophilus, 348/347 (Diogenes Laertius III.2).

occasions.label: Aristotle leaves Athens and the Academy, with Xenocrates, for the court of Hermias
occasions.note: Why he left is not known: Speusippus' succession and the hostility to Macedon after Olynthus fell (348) are the two explanations.

occasions.label: Demosthenes on the embassy to Philip; the Peace of Philocrates
occasions.note: The two embassies of 346, from the spring to the oaths at Pella in the summer.

occasions.label: Isocrates' Philippus calls on Philip to unite the Greeks against Persia
occasions.note: Written soon after the Peace of Philocrates.

occasions.label: Aristotle on Lesbos with Theophrastus: their studies of animals and plants
Philip calls Aristotle to teach Alexander, then thirteen
Demosthenes' Third Philippic
Hermias betrayed to the Persians and executed
occasions.note: Aristotle honoured him with a hymn and an epigram at Delphi.

occasions.label: Death of Speusippus; the Academy elects Xenocrates
Philip defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea; Alexander leads the charge; Demosthenes fights in the ranks and flees
occasions.note: 7 Metageitnion (Plutarch, Camillus 19), about the beginning of August 338 BC.

occasions.label: Death of Isocrates, aged ninety-eight, days after Chaeronea
occasions.note: That he starved himself on the news of the battle is tradition.

occasions.label: Demosthenes chosen to speak over the dead of Chaeronea
occasions.note: On the Crown 285.

occasions.label: At Philip's wedding to Cleopatra, Alexander quarrels with his father and leaves Macedon
Philip murdered by Pausanias at his daughter's wedding; Alexander succeeds and buries him
Demosthenes appears garlanded in the assembly at the news, and mocks Alexander as a boy
occasions.note: Plutarch, Demosthenes 22; Aeschines, Against Ctesiphon 77 and 160.

occasions.label: Alexander visits Diogenes, who asks him to stand out of his sun
occasions.note: An anecdote (Plutarch, Alexander 14; Diogenes Laertius VI.38); its historicity is doubted.

occasions.label: Alexander destroys Thebes and demands the Athenian orators, Demosthenes first; Demades talks him round
Aristotle returns to Athens and teaches in the Lyceum, Theophrastus with him, as a rival to the Academy
On the Crown: the jury vindicates Demosthenes against Aeschines
After the death of Callisthenes, Aristotle's kinsman, Alexander writes that he will punish the sophist who sent him
occasions.note: Plutarch, Alexander 55.

occasions.label: Convicted of taking Harpalus' gold, Demosthenes is fined and escapes into exile
occasions.note: Harpalus came to Athens in 324; the Areopagus reported after six months, and the trials followed early in 323.

occasions.label: Death of Alexander, recorded by the Babylonian astronomers
occasions.note: 29 Aiaru: the evening of 10 or 11 June 323 BC.

occasions.label: In the revolt after Alexander's death Athens recalls Demosthenes from exile
Charged with impiety, Aristotle leaves Athens for Chalcis, leaving the Lyceum to Theophrastus
occasions.note: His saying that he would not let Athens sin twice against philosophy is late tradition.

occasions.label: Death of Aristotle
occasions.note: In the archonship of Philocles, 322/321 (Apollodorus in Diogenes Laertius V.10), and so in the second half of 322 BC.

occasions.label: Hunted by Antipater's men, Demosthenes takes poison in the temple of Poseidon
occasions.note: 16 Pyanepsion, in October 322 BC.

ties.note: The assembly re-elected him general in 429, shortly before his death.
Plutarch (Pericles 36) tells of a whole day they spent arguing who was to blame for an accidental death at the games.
Anaxagoras taught Pericles (Plato, Phaedrus 270a).
The city that had harboured him for thirty years prosecutes him, and he leaves.
His accusers held the careers of Alcibiades and Critias against Socrates (Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.2.12).
At Arginusae he opposed the assembly in the name of its own laws: the act of opposition is coded (codebook §6, mixed acts).
Plato's Symposium shows them at one table in 416 in good humour; that is a dramatic setting, not coded.
The Frogs (405) went on with the parody after his death.
Sophocles' chorus in mourning for Euripides at the proagon of 406 is a regard shown after the end of the tie, and so not coded.
The Seventh Letter calls Socrates the most just man of his time (324e).
Critias had been one of Socrates' companions; under the Thirty he forbade him to teach.
Plato's revulsion from his kinsmen's rule rests on the Seventh Letter.
Between his flight in 415 and his recall by the fleet at Samos in 411 he served Sparta and then Tissaphernes.
Plato offended the tyrant by his frankness; the sale into slavery is doubted.
Dion was the brother of Dionysius' wife Aristomache, and married his daughter.
The tyrant wanted Plato's regard to the end; the break of 361 is the act remembered.
Dion was the young tyrant's uncle and chief counsellor until his banishment.
Twenty years of pupillage; the anecdotes of a quarrel (Diogenes Laertius V.2) are late.
Contested: whether he left in 347 for disappointment at Speusippus' succession or for fear of anti-Macedonian feeling; the Lyceum is a rival school, but he still wrote of 'we' Platonists.
Diogenes Laertius has him come to Athens 'to vex Plato, who had passed him over'; his astronomy and his hedonism were discussed in the Academy.
Aristotle married Pythias, Hermias' niece or adopted daughter.
Aristotle's will leaves him his library and the school.
A metic in Athens; the charge was brought by the hierophant Eurymedon.
The later rumour that Aristotle had a part in poisoning Alexander is rejected.
Father and son were reconciled before the murder; Alexander buried his father and punished the conspirators.
On the embassy of 346 Demosthenes worked for the peace; Aeschines says he broke down before Philip (On the Embassy 34-35).
In 335 Alexander relented and asked only for Charidemus' exile.
If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes: an anecdote. Demetrius had them die on the same day (Diogenes Laertius VI.79).
